title: Connectors & Registries
summary: You rarely have to build every tool your agent needs. A growing ecosystem of pre-built MCP servers (connectors) exposes ready-made tools for GitHub, Slack, databases, and more, and registries index them so you can discover and install one in minutes. But installing a third-party server means running someone else's code with your agent's permissions, so the same supply-chain concerns as any dependency apply: you evaluate trust, pin versions, and treat an unvetted connector as an attack surface — deciding install-vs-build on capability, risk, and maintenance rather than convenience alone.

subtopics.title: Connectors are pre-built MCP servers
subtopics.explanation: A connector is an MCP server someone already wrote that packages tools for a specific system — a GitHub connector exposes create_issue and list_prs, a Postgres connector exposes run_query. Your agent speaks the standard MCP protocol to it, so any MCP-aware host can use it without custom glue. Connectors matter because they turn 'integrate with service X' from a coding project into a configuration step.

subtopics.title: Registries let you discover connectors
subtopics.explanation: A registry is an index of available MCP servers with metadata — name, description, publisher, tools exposed, and version — so you can search for a capability instead of hunting through repos. It is the package-index layer of the MCP ecosystem, analogous to npm or PyPI for tools. Registries matter because discovery and trust signals (downloads, publisher, provenance) are what make an ecosystem usable at scale.
subtopics.example:
# pseudo-code: query a registry for a capability
hits = registry.search("send slack message")
for s in hits:
    print(s.name, s.publisher, s.version, s.verified)
# slack-connector   acme-labs   1.4.2   True
# slackbot-tools     random-dev  0.0.3   False  <- weaker trust signals
chosen = next(s for s in hits if s.verified)  # prefer vetted publishers

subtopics.title: Deciding install vs build
subtopics.explanation: Installing a connector is fast and maintained by others; building your own is more work but gives you full control over scope, dependencies, and behavior. You lean toward installing for common, well-vetted integrations and toward building when the connector is unmaintained, over-privileged, or touches sensitive systems. The decision is a trade-off among capability, risk, and long-term maintenance, not just today's convenience.

subtopics.title: Trust and supply-chain risk
subtopics.explanation: A third-party connector runs as code inside (or adjacent to) your agent and often holds credentials, so a malicious or compromised one can exfiltrate secrets, take unwanted actions, or inject prompt content through tool results. This is the classic software supply-chain problem plus a new prompt-injection surface. Treating every connector as untrusted code — reviewing it, sandboxing it, and scoping its credentials — is the core safety discipline of using the ecosystem.
subtopics.example:
# defensive posture around a third-party connector
connector = load_connector("some-third-party/pdf-tools")

# 1. scope credentials narrowly (read-only, single repo, short TTL)
token = mint_token(scopes=["repo:read"], ttl_minutes=30)
# 2. run it sandboxed with no ambient network/filesystem access
sandbox = Sandbox(network="deny", fs="readonly")
# 3. treat tool_result text as untrusted (possible prompt injection)
result = sandbox.run(connector, token=token)
safe = sanitize_untrusted(result)  # never blindly trust returned content

subtopics.title: Versioning and pinning
subtopics.explanation: Connectors evolve, and an auto-updating dependency can silently change a tool's behavior, arguments, or permissions overnight — breaking your agent or widening its access. You pin exact versions, review changelogs before upgrading, and re-test the agent against the new version like any dependency bump. Pinning is what makes a third-party tool's behavior reproducible and its upgrades a deliberate, reviewable event.

foundations.overview: Connectors and registries are the ecosystem layer of MCP. A connector is a pre-built MCP server that exposes ready-made tools for a system (GitHub, Slack, Postgres, Google Drive), letting any MCP-aware agent use those tools without writing integration code. Registries are searchable indexes of these servers — the package-index layer — carrying metadata and trust signals (publisher, version, verification, popularity) so you can discover a capability instead of building it. The payoff is speed: integrating a service becomes configuration, not a coding project. The cost is that installing a connector means running third-party code with your agent's credentials, so every classic software supply-chain risk applies plus a new one — tool results are attacker-influenceable text that can carry prompt injection. Mature usage therefore weighs install-vs-build on capability, risk, and maintenance; scopes credentials narrowly; sandboxes untrusted servers; treats returned content as untrusted; and pins exact versions so upgrades are deliberate, reviewed events rather than silent behavior changes.
foundations.formalDefinition: A connector is a reusable MCP server implementation that exposes a fixed set of tools/resources for an external system over the MCP protocol. A registry is an indexed catalog of connectors with discovery metadata (name, publisher, version, exposed tools, trust signals). Adopting a connector is a dependency decision governed by trust evaluation, credential scoping, sandboxing, and version pinning to bound supply-chain and prompt-injection risk.
foundations.whyItMatters: Connectors turn the slowest part of building an agent — wiring it to real systems — into minutes of configuration, which is why the MCP ecosystem is exploding. But because each connector runs with real credentials and can influence the model through its outputs, treating them casually is how agents leak secrets or take harmful actions; the discipline around trust and versioning is what keeps the speed from becoming a liability.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of connectors like npm packages for your agent's hands. A registry is the package index; installing is a one-line add that saves days of work — but you would never run an unvetted package with your production credentials and auto-update it nightly, and a connector is exactly that, except it can also whisper instructions into your model through its tool results.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Teams install official connectors for GitHub, Slack, Google Drive, and databases to stand up an agent in an afternoon, discover niche tools through registries, pin versions in their MCP config, and build custom in-house connectors for sensitive systems (payments, PII stores) where they need tight scope control.
commonUseCases: Standing up common integrations (GitHub, Slack, DB) fast
Discovering niche tools via a registry search
Choosing install-vs-build for a sensitive integration
Pinning and reviewing connector versions in CI

commonMisconceptions.myth: A pre-built connector is safe because it's popular or official-looking.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Popularity is a weak signal. Connectors run with your credentials and their outputs can carry prompt injection, so you still scope tokens, sandbox, review code, and pin versions.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Installing a connector is always better than building one.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Installing wins for common, vetted, low-risk tools; for sensitive systems needing tight scope, an unmaintained or over-privileged connector is worse than a small custom build you control.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Once installed, a connector's behavior is fixed.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Unpinned connectors auto-update and can silently change tool behavior, arguments, or permission scope; pin exact versions and treat upgrades as reviewed changes.

interactiveWidget.title: Install-vs-build, at a glance
interactiveWidget.caption: A quick decision aid: when a pre-built connector is the right call, when to build your own, and the guardrails either way.

config.note: INSTALL a connector when the integration is common, the publisher is verified, the tool is well-maintained, and it does not touch sensitive data (e.g. a public-docs search or a read-only GitHub connector). BUILD your own when the connector is unmaintained or over-privileged, or when it touches PII, payments, or internal systems that demand tightly scoped permissions — a small tool you own beats a broad one you don't. EITHER WAY: (1) scope credentials to the minimum (read-only, single resource, short TTL); (2) pin the EXACT version — never '@latest' — so upgrades are deliberate, reviewed events; (3) sandbox third-party servers with no ambient network/filesystem access; (4) treat every tool_result as UNTRUSTED text that may contain prompt injection, and sanitize before acting on it. Mental model: a connector is an npm package for your agent's hands — huge time savings, but you would never run an unvetted, auto-updating package with production credentials.

checkpoints.prompt: What is a 'connector' in the MCP ecosystem?
options: A network cable spec for agents
A pre-built MCP server exposing ready-made tools for a system
checkpoints.explanation: A connector is a reusable MCP server that packages tools for a specific system (GitHub, Slack, a database), so any MCP-aware agent can use those tools without writing integration code.

checkpoints.prompt: Which factor most argues for BUILDING your own connector instead of installing one?
options: The integration is common and popular
It touches PII/payments and needs tightly scoped permissions
checkpoints.explanation: Sensitive systems needing tight scope favor a small connector you control. Common, verified, popular, well-downloaded tools are exactly the cases where installing is the better trade-off.

checkpoints.prompt: What's the supply-chain risk in this connector config?
options: '@latest' auto-updates behavior silently AND the token has full admin scope — a compromised update inherits broad access
checkpoints.explanation: Two compounding risks: a floating '@latest' lets a malicious or breaking update land without review, and a broad admin token means that update inherits full access. Pin the version and scope the token minimally.

keyTakeaways: Connectors are pre-built MCP servers that turn 'integrate with service X' into configuration instead of a coding project.
Registries index connectors with trust signals (publisher, version, verification) so you can discover capabilities, like a package index for tools.
Decide install-vs-build on capability, risk, and maintenance: install common vetted low-risk tools; build sensitive ones you must tightly scope.
A third-party connector is untrusted code with your credentials AND a prompt-injection surface via tool results — scope tokens, sandbox, and sanitize outputs.
Pin exact connector versions (never '@latest') so behavior is reproducible and upgrades are deliberate, reviewed events.
